OpenConsole

Share a terminal. No inbound ports.

What it is Using it Why it is useful Security What it is not

What it is

OpenConsole hands someone else your terminal. You run one command, it prints a link, and whoever opens that link sees the same shell you are typing in — and can type into it too, if you let them.

Neither end has to be reachable from the internet. Both dial out to a relay, which brokers bytes between the one terminal being shared and everyone watching it. Nothing listens on your machine, no port is opened, no firewall rule changes. 

    your machine                 relay                   a guest
  ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
  │  shell on a  │  dials  │              │  dials  │   browser,   │
  │ pty / ConPTY │ ──────▶ │   brokers    │ ◀────── │  CLI or ssh  │
  │              │   out   │    bytes     │   out   │              │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘

The relay never executes anything. It is a switchboard: it knows a session exists and who is attached to it, and — when the session is encrypted, which is the default — it cannot read a byte of what goes through it.

Using it

Share your terminal

Install the client, then run it:

curl -fsSL https://openconsole.dev/install.sh | sh
openconsole

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https://openconsole.dev/install.ps1 | iex
openconsole

It prints a link and a ticket. Send either to whoever is joining. When you exit the shell, the session ends. On Windows this shares cmd.exe; add -shell powershell.exe for PowerShell.

Join someone else's

Open the link in a browser — nothing to install, which is the point. From a terminal, openconsole join <ticket>. A stock ssh client works too, if the host turned encryption off for that reason.

Let someone watch without typing

Every session also produces a watch-only link. Hand that one out when somebody only needs to see. It is not a setting the relay is trusted to honour — see Security.

Reach a port on the host

A guest can forward a TCP port through the same connection, so a database or a dev server on the host becomes reachable locally: 

openconsole -allow-forward localhost:5432          # what the host permits
openconsole join <ticket> -L 5432:localhost:5432  # what the guest asks for

Forwarding is off unless the host asks for it, and the host names what may be reached. A forward reaches whatever that machine can reach, which is why it is never on by default.

Why it is useful

  • Nothing to install to join. A browser is enough. The person you are helping does not have to set anything up before you can help them.
  • No inbound ports, no VPN, no firewall change. Both ends dial out. This works from a laptop behind NAT, a container, or a locked-down corporate network.
  • It is the real terminal. Full-screen programs, colours, arrow keys and Ctrl-C — not a recording, not a video stream. Guests see the shell as it happens, at the size the host's window actually is.
  • Pairing, debugging, teaching, support. Anywhere the useful thing is "look at what my machine is doing", rather than screenshots and copied-out log lines.
  • You can run the relay yourself. One binary, one container image. Then the only machines involved are yours.

Security

You are giving somebody a shell. That deserves a straight account of who can see what, so here is one, including the parts that are not reassuring.

The relay cannot read your terminal

Sessions are end-to-end encrypted by default, with AES-256-GCM. The key is generated on the host and the relay is never told it: it lives in the ticket, which travels to your guest out of band, and in the link's fragment, which browsers do not send to servers. There is no key exchange, so there is nothing for the relay to interpose on. It routes ciphertext.

Watch-only is arithmetic, not a rule

Two keys are derived from that root, one per direction. A full guest gets the root and can derive both. A viewer is given only the host-to-guest key — enough to read the terminal, and not enough to produce input the host will accept. Read-only does not depend on the relay behaving itself; a viewer cannot type because the arithmetic will not do it.

What is still visible to the relay

Contents are hidden; shape is not. The relay can see that a session exists, when someone joined, how large each burst of output is, and when. It can also drop or reorder frames — which breaks a session rather than falsifying one. Padding and cover traffic are not attempted.

A link is a bearer capability

Anyone who has the whole link has the terminal. There is no per-guest identity, no audit trail, and no way to revoke one link short of ending the session. Treat it like a password: send it over something you trust, and end the session when you are done.

Turning encryption off

-no-encryption exists for exactly one reason: a stock ssh client has no key and cannot decrypt. It hands the relay everything encryption withholds — it can then read the terminal and inject keystrokes. Use it when the ssh path is what you need, and know what you are trading.

If you run the relay

Terminate TLS in front of it: tokens are bearer credentials and the code assumes a proxy is doing that. Session creation is unauthenticated by default — rate limited and capped, but open — and OPENCONSOLE_CREATE_TOKEN closes it. Sessions live in memory only, expire on a TTL, and nothing is written to disk.

What it is not

It is not audited, and it is not yet something to expose to the public internet without reading the gaps first. They are written down rather than glossed over: known gaps.

It is not a screen share, a recording tool, or a way to reach a machine that is switched off. The host has to be running the command for a session to exist at all.
